immigrant.simple: A person who comes to live permanently in a new country.
immigrant.detailed: Someone who leaves their home country and settles in another, often for work, safety, or family reasons.
immigrant.example: Many immigrant families in Melbourne keep stories of the voyage that brought them to Australia.
immigrant.basic: Many families came from another country to live here.

insulator.simple: A material that slows heat, electricity, or sound from passing through.
insulator.detailed: A substance used to reduce the transfer of heat or electric current, such as rubber around a wire or wool in a jumper.
insulator.example: Wool is a useful insulator because it traps air and keeps heat from escaping the jumper.
insulator.basic: Wool helps stop heat from getting out of the jumper.

laboratory.simple: A room where scientists test ideas and carry out careful experiments.
laboratory.detailed: A specially equipped workspace for investigating materials, living things, or physical changes under controlled conditions.
laboratory.example: The class moved into the laboratory to test which fabric kept water warm the longest.
laboratory.basic: The class went to the science room to test the fabrics.

liquid.simple: A substance that flows and takes the shape of its container.
liquid.detailed: One of the main states of matter, with a fixed volume but no fixed shape, such as water or oil at room temperature.
liquid.example: Water is a liquid at room temperature, but it becomes ice when it freezes.
liquid.basic: Water can be poured at room temperature.

magnet.simple: An object that pulls iron or steel towards it.
magnet.detailed: A material or device that produces a magnetic field, attracting ferromagnetic metals and aligning a compass with Earth's poles.
magnet.example: The north pole of one magnet pushed the other magnet away during the force test.
magnet.basic: One metal bar pushed the other metal bar away.

mass.simple: How much matter is in an object, measured in grams or kilograms.
mass.detailed: A scientific measure of the quantity of matter in an object, which stays the same even if weight changes with gravity.
mass.example: The mass of the rock stayed the same in the thought experiment about Earth and the Moon.
mass.basic: The amount of stuff in the rock did not change.

matter.simple: Anything that has mass and takes up space.
matter.detailed: The material that makes up objects, existing as solid, liquid, or gas, and made of particles that can be measured.
matter.example: Scientists classify matter by whether it keeps its shape or can be poured.
matter.basic: Scientists group stuff by how it behaves.

metaphor.simple: A comparison that says one thing is another to create a strong image.
metaphor.detailed: A figurative comparison made without like or as, used to suggest a deeper likeness between two unlike things.
metaphor.example: Calling the drought a thief is a metaphor that makes the land's loss feel personal.
metaphor.basic: The writer said the drought stole from the land.

migration.simple: The movement of people or animals from one place to another to live.
migration.detailed: A large-scale shift of people or species between regions, often seasonal or caused by work, climate, or conflict.
migration.example: The inquiry compared bird migration along the coast with human movement after Federation.
migration.basic: The class compared how birds and people move to new places.

mixture.simple: Two or more substances put together that can often be separated again.
mixture.detailed: A physical combination of materials in which each keeps its own properties, unlike a new chemical compound.
mixture.example: Sand and iron filings form a mixture that a magnet can separate.
mixture.basic: Sand and iron bits can be put together and then pulled apart.

molecule.simple: The smallest unit of a substance that still has that substance's properties.
molecule.detailed: A group of two or more atoms bonded together, such as water made of hydrogen joined to oxygen.
molecule.example: A water molecule is made of two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom.
molecule.basic: The smallest bit of water is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom.

monument.simple: A building or statue made to honour a person or event.
monument.detailed: A lasting public structure that commemorates history, often visited as a civic or heritage site.
monument.example: The class sketched the war monument before writing about how towns remember soldiers.
monument.basic: The class sketched the statue that remembers the soldiers.

mood.simple: The feeling a story or place creates in the reader.
mood.detailed: The atmosphere built through setting, word choice, and imagery, such as tense, joyful, or gloomy.
mood.example: Fog and short sentences built a tense mood as the campers lost the track.
mood.basic: The scene felt tense when the campers got lost.

nation.simple: A large group of people who share a country and often a government.
nation.detailed: A political community living under one system of laws, sometimes also bound by language, history, or culture.
nation.example: After Federation, the colonies joined to form one nation with a shared parliament.
nation.basic: The colonies joined to make one country.

narrator.simple: The voice that tells the story to the reader.
narrator.detailed: The person or character who reports events, which may be a first-person speaker or an outside observer.
narrator.example: The narrator whispered secrets the other characters could not hear.
narrator.basic: The storyteller knew things the characters did not.

nutrient.simple: A substance in food that living things need to grow and stay healthy.
nutrient.detailed: A chemical such as a protein, mineral, or vitamin that organisms absorb to build cells and release energy.
nutrient.example: Plants take a nutrient such as nitrogen from the soil through their roots.
nutrient.basic: Plants take useful substances from the soil.

organism.simple: A living thing, such as a plant, animal, or microbe.
organism.detailed: An individual life form that can grow, respond, and, in most cases, reproduce, from a bacterium to a whale.
organism.example: Every organism in the rock-pool food web depends on energy that began with sunlight.
organism.basic: Every living thing in the rock pool needs energy from the sun.

oxygen.simple: The gas in air that most living things need to breathe.
oxygen.detailed: A colourless element that supports combustion and respiration, and is released by plants when they make food from light.
oxygen.example: Fish take oxygen from the water through their gills.
oxygen.basic: Fish take the breathable gas they need from the water.

parliament.simple: A group of elected people who make a country's laws.
parliament.detailed: In Australia, the national law-making body in Canberra, with the House of Representatives and the Senate.
parliament.example: Federal parliament meets in Canberra to debate bills that can become law.
parliament.basic: The country's law-makers meet in Canberra.

particle.simple: A tiny bit of matter, often too small to see clearly.
particle.detailed: A minute portion of a substance, from a dust speck to the atoms and molecules used in science explanations.
particle.example: A dust particle in the sunbeam showed that air is not empty.
particle.basic: A tiny speck of dust floated in the sunlight.

photosynthesis.simple: The way green plants make food from sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide.
photosynthesis.detailed: The process in leaf cells that turns light energy into stored chemical energy and releases oxygen as a by-product.
photosynthesis.example: Leaves look green because the pigment that drives photosynthesis reflects green light.
photosynthesis.basic: Leaves look green because the pigment that helps plants make food reflects green light.

planet.simple: A large round object that orbits a star, such as Earth around the Sun.
planet.detailed: A celestial body that travels around a star and does not produce its own light, distinguished from moons and stars.
planet.example: Earth is the only planet in our solar system known to have liquid water on its surface.
planet.basic: Earth is the only world near the Sun with seas of water.

plot.simple: The chain of events that make up a story.
plot.detailed: The ordered sequence of complications, turning points, and resolution that carries a narrative forward.
plot.example: The plot thickened when the missing map turned up in the antagonist's tent.
plot.basic: The story got more complicated when the map appeared.

pollution.simple: Harmful substances released into air, water, or land.
pollution.detailed: Contamination of the environment by waste, chemicals, or noise that damages living systems and human health.
pollution.example: Creek testing showed pollution after heavy rain washed litter into the water.
pollution.basic: The creek was dirtied after rain washed rubbish in.

predator.simple: An animal that hunts other animals for food.
predator.detailed: An organism that captures and consumes prey, shaping food webs and the size of other populations.
predator.example: The owl is a night predator that hunts mice in the grassland.
predator.basic: The owl hunts mice at night.

prejudice.simple: An unfair opinion formed before knowing the facts.
prejudice.detailed: A fixed, usually negative judgement about a group or person, based on stereotype rather than evidence.
prejudice.example: The novel shows how prejudice stops neighbours from listening to one another.
prejudice.basic: Unfair ideas stopped the neighbours from listening.

prey.simple: An animal hunted by another animal for food.
prey.detailed: An organism captured and eaten by a predator, often adapted to hide, flee, or defend itself.
prey.example: Mice become prey when the owl's silent flight brings it over the grass.
prey.basic: Mice are the animals the owl tries to catch.

producer.simple: A living thing, usually a plant, that makes its own food from sunlight.
producer.detailed: In a food web, an organism that converts light or chemical energy into stored food that consumers later use.
producer.example: Seagrass is a producer that feeds the whole shallow-water food web.
producer.basic: Seagrass makes food that other sea animals depend on.

protagonist.simple: The main character the story follows most closely.
protagonist.detailed: The central figure whose goals and struggles drive the plot, often contrasted with an antagonist.
protagonist.example: The protagonist had to choose honesty even when it cost the team the trophy.
protagonist.basic: The main character had to tell the truth.

reaction.simple: A change that happens when substances or forces act on each other.
reaction.detailed: In science, a chemical process that forms new substances, or a physical response to a stimulus.
reaction.example: The vinegar and bicarbonate produced a fizzing reaction and a burst of gas.
reaction.basic: The vinegar and bicarbonate fizzed and made gas.

reproduction.simple: The process living things use to make more of their own kind.
reproduction.detailed: The biological production of offspring, which may be sexual or asexual, keeping a species going over time.
reproduction.example: Frog reproduction depends on a wet place where eggs will not dry out.
reproduction.basic: Frogs need a wet place to have young.

rights.simple: Freedoms and protections a person is entitled to by law or fairness.
rights.detailed: Legal or moral entitlements, such as the right to education or a fair hearing, often set out in charters.
rights.example: The inquiry asked which rights children can expect at school and in the community.
rights.basic: The class asked what protections children should have.

sediment.simple: Bits of rock, soil, or shell that settle at the bottom of water.
sediment.detailed: Material eroded and carried by water, wind, or ice, then deposited in layers that may later form sedimentary rock.
sediment.example: After the flood, a thick layer of sediment covered the creek path.
sediment.basic: After the flood, mud settled over the path.

settlement.simple: A place where people have come to live and build a community.
settlement.detailed: A community established in a new area, or the act of people making a home there; in Australian HASS this often refers to colonial towns.
settlement.example: The goldfield settlement grew from tents into shops and a school.
settlement.basic: The goldfield camp grew into a small town.

simile.simple: A comparison that uses like or as to show how two things are alike.
simile.detailed: A figurative device that makes an image clearer by linking unlike things with the words like or as.
simile.example: The simile “the creek was as brown as tea” helped readers picture the floodwater.
simile.basic: Saying the creek was as brown as tea helped readers picture it.

society.simple: People living together under shared rules and customs.
society.detailed: An organised community of people with institutions, culture, and relationships that shape daily life.
society.example: Rules about sharing water show how a society manages a scarce resource.
society.basic: Rules about sharing water show how a community manages a shortage.

solid.simple: A substance that keeps its own shape and does not flow.
solid.detailed: A state of matter with a definite shape and volume because particles are packed in a fixed arrangement.
solid.example: Ice is a solid, so it holds its shape until heat turns it into water.
solid.basic: Ice keeps its shape until it melts.

species.simple: A group of living things that can breed and produce young of the same kind.
species.detailed: A rank in biological classification grouping organisms that share key traits and, usually, can interbreed.
species.example: The platypus is a species found only in eastern Australia.
species.basic: The platypus is a kind of animal found only in eastern Australia.

symbol.simple: An object or image that stands for a bigger idea.
symbol.detailed: A concrete sign—flag, colour, or object—used to represent an abstract value, group, or theme.
symbol.example: The wattle is a symbol of Australia on the national coat of arms.
symbol.basic: The wattle stands for Australia on the coat of arms.

temperature.simple: A measure of how hot or cold something is.
temperature.detailed: A measure of the average kinetic energy of particles, recorded in degrees Celsius in Australian classrooms.
temperature.example: They recorded the temperature of the water every ten minutes during the insulation test.
temperature.basic: They wrote down how hot the water was every ten minutes.

texture.simple: How a surface feels, or looks as if it would feel.
texture.detailed: The tactile or visual quality of a material—rough, smooth, grainy—used in science and in descriptive writing.
texture.example: The sandstone's rough texture showed grains that had been cemented together.
texture.basic: The sandstone felt rough because of the tiny grains.

tone.simple: The writer's attitude toward the subject or the reader.
tone.detailed: The stance expressed through word choice and rhythm—serious, playful, bitter—which shapes how a text feels.
tone.example: A sarcastic tone made the letter funny, but it also risked sounding unkind.
tone.basic: The letter sounded mocking, which made it funny and a bit unkind.

tradition.simple: A custom passed down through families or communities.
tradition.detailed: A practice, story, or belief kept over generations because it expresses identity or shared values.
tradition.example: Sharing stories around the fire is a tradition in many First Nations communities.
tradition.basic: Sharing stories around the fire is a long-kept custom.

treaty.simple: A formal written agreement between countries or groups.
treaty.detailed: A negotiated legal pact that sets rights, borders, or peace terms, binding the parties that sign it.
treaty.example: Students compared a peace treaty with a classroom contract to see how promises are written down.
treaty.basic: Students compared a peace agreement with a classroom contract.

vapour.simple: A gas form of a substance that is usually liquid or solid.
vapour.detailed: The gaseous state of a material such as water, often seen as steam or as an invisible gas above a liquid.
vapour.example: Water vapour in the warm air condensed on the cold glass of the window.
vapour.basic: Invisible wetness in the warm air turned to drops on the cold glass.

weathering.simple: The slow breaking down of rocks by weather, water, or plants.
weathering.detailed: Physical or chemical decay of rock in place, caused by temperature change, water, wind, or living things, before erosion carries pieces away.
weathering.example: Cracks from ice expanding in winter are a form of physical weathering.
weathering.basic: Ice in the cracks slowly breaks the rock apart.

area.simple: A particular part of a place, or the size of a surface.
area.detailed: In HASS, a district or region under discussion; in measurement, the amount of space a surface covers.
area.example: The local area around the creek includes farmland, bush, and a small town.
area.basic: The land around the creek includes farms, bush, and a town.

aspect.simple: One part or feature of a larger idea or problem.
aspect.detailed: A particular side of a topic that can be examined on its own, such as the cost side of a plan.
aspect.example: Cost was only one aspect of the waste plan; fairness mattered too.
aspect.basic: Cost was only one part of the waste plan.

chapter.simple: A numbered section of a book that groups related events.
chapter.detailed: A major division of a long text, often with its own focus, that moves the whole work forward.
chapter.example: The last chapter revealed why the narrator had hidden the letter.
chapter.basic: The last part of the book explained the hidden letter.

clause.simple: A group of words with a subject and a verb, often part of a longer sentence.
clause.detailed: A grammatical unit that can stand alone as a sentence or join another unit with a conjunction.
clause.example: A dependent clause cannot stand alone, even if it contains a verb.
clause.basic: Some groups of words need to join another sentence to make sense.

component.simple: One working part that belongs to a larger whole.
component.detailed: An essential piece of a system, machine, or mixture whose role can be named and tested.
component.example: The battery is a component of the circuit that supplies the energy.
component.basic: The battery is one working part of the circuit.

contract.simple: A formal agreement that people or groups promise to follow.
contract.detailed: A legally binding document that sets out duties, payment, and rights for the parties who sign it.
contract.example: The council published the cleaning contract so residents could see what had been promised.
contract.basic: The council shared the written cleaning agreement.

creation.simple: The act of making something new, or the thing that was made.
creation.detailed: The process of inventing or producing a work, idea, or object, and the product that results.
creation.example: The creation of the Federation flag involved choosing symbols both sides could accept.
creation.basic: Making the Federation flag meant choosing symbols both sides could accept.

decade.simple: A period of ten years, used to group history.
decade.detailed: A ten-year span used to group historical change, such as the 1890s or the past ten years.
decade.example: In one decade the goldfield town grew from tents to brick shops.
decade.basic: In ten years the goldfield town grew from tents to brick shops.

description.simple: Words that tell how a person, place, or thing looks, sounds, or feels.
description.detailed: An account that uses sensory language and precise facts so a reader can picture the subject clearly.
description.example: Her description of the storm used sound as well as colour so readers could feel it.
description.basic: She wrote about the storm so readers could picture it.

development.simple: Growth or change that makes something more advanced over time.
development.detailed: Progress in a place, idea, or skill, including economic growth, new building, or a story moving forward.
development.example: Railway development linked the inland town to the port within twenty years.
development.basic: Building the railway linked the inland town to the port.

equation.simple: A number sentence that shows two sides are equal.
equation.detailed: A mathematical statement that two expressions have the same value, solved by finding the unknown.
equation.example: They wrote an equation to show how mass and volume relate to density.
equation.basic: They wrote a number sentence to show how mass and volume relate.

export.simple: A good sent to another country to be sold.
export.detailed: A product or service produced in one country and sold abroad, important to trade and national income.
export.example: Wool was once Australia's most famous export to Britain.
export.basic: Wool was once Australia's most famous product sold overseas.

framework.simple: A basic structure that holds ideas or parts in order.
framework.detailed: An organised set of rules, ideas, or supports used to plan thinking, writing, or a physical system.
framework.example: The PEEL framework helped Oliver organise each persuasive paragraph.
framework.basic: The PEEL structure helped him organise each persuasive paragraph.

income.simple: Money received from work, sales, or other sources.
income.detailed: Regular earnings of a person, family, or country, used to pay for goods, services, and savings.
income.example: The inquiry compared farm income in a drought year with income after good rain.
income.basic: The class compared what farmers earned in a dry year and a wet year.

instance.simple: A single example of something happening or being true.
instance.detailed: A particular case used to illustrate a general idea, often introduced with for example.
instance.example: One instance of kindness was the neighbour who filled the water tanks.
instance.basic: One example of kindness was the neighbour who filled the tanks.

labour.simple: Work, especially hard or paid work done by people.
labour.detailed: Human effort used to produce goods and services; also the workers as a group in an economy.
labour.example: Building the railway took years of hard labour in heat and dust.
labour.basic: Building the railway took years of hard work in heat and dust.

legislation.simple: A set of laws made by a parliament or similar body.
legislation.detailed: Written statutes passed by a legislature that set rules the public must follow.
legislation.example: New water legislation limited how much each farm could pump from the river.
legislation.basic: A new law limited how much each farm could pump from the river.

percent.simple: A number of parts out of every hundred, shown with %.
percent.detailed: A rate expressed per hundred, written with the % sign, used to compare quantities fairly.
percent.example: Forty percent of the class walked to school after the new path opened.
percent.basic: Two-fifths of the class walked to school after the path opened.

percentage.simple: An amount written as a share of every hundred parts.
percentage.detailed: A proportion expressed out of 100, used in data, chance, and fair comparison.
percentage.example: A small percentage of plastic bottles was actually recycled at the school.
percentage.basic: Only a small share of the bottles was actually recycled.

region.simple: A large area of land that shares features or a name.
region.detailed: A geographic district defined by nature, culture, or government, larger than a town and smaller than a continent.
region.example: The Murray–Darling is a farming region that depends on river water.
region.basic: The Murray–Darling is a farming area that depends on the river.

sector.simple: One part of the economy or of a community's work.
sector.detailed: A grouping of jobs or activities, such as farming or government services, used when discussing how a country works.
sector.example: Jobs in the farming sector fell during the long drought.
sector.basic: Farm jobs fell during the long drought.

site.simple: The place where something is built or where an event happened.
site.detailed: A specific location used for a building, an investigation, or a historical event.
site.example: The heritage site still shows the foundations of the first schoolhouse.
site.basic: You can still see the foundations of the first schoolhouse there.

text.simple: A piece of writing that can be read and discussed.
text.detailed: Any written, spoken, or visual work studied for meaning, including articles, poems, and reports.
text.example: The information text used headings and diagrams to explain the water cycle.
text.basic: The information piece used headings and diagrams to explain the water cycle.

version.simple: One form of something that also exists in other forms.
version.detailed: A particular edition, retelling, or variant of a text, plan, or product.
version.example: Oliver preferred the first version of his speech because it sounded more honest.
version.basic: He preferred the first draft of his speech because it sounded more honest.

additional.simple: Extra; more than the amount you already have.
additional.detailed: Further or supplementary, added to an amount, list, or argument that already exists.
additional.example: The marker wanted additional evidence, not just one short example.
additional.basic: The marker wanted extra evidence, not just one short example.

ancient.simple: Belonging to a time many centuries ago, not today.
ancient.detailed: Dating from the distant past, often thousands of years, and contrasted with modern life.
ancient.example: The inquiry compared ancient trade routes with shipping lanes used today.
ancient.basic: The class compared very old trade routes with shipping lanes used today.

annual.simple: Happening once every year, or measured over a year.
annual.detailed: Occurring yearly, or measured over a twelve-month period, such as a yearly report or rainfall total.
annual.example: The town's annual rainfall fell sharply during the drought years.
annual.basic: The town's yearly rainfall fell sharply during the drought.

apparent.simple: Easy to see or understand; seeming to be true.
apparent.detailed: Clear from the evidence, or appearing true on the surface even if later checks prove otherwise.
apparent.example: It became apparent that the leak, not evaporation, had emptied the tank.
apparent.basic: It became clear that the leak, not evaporation, had emptied the tank.

appropriate.simple: Right or suitable for this situation and audience.
appropriate.detailed: Fitting the purpose, audience, or rules, so the choice is judged fair and sensible.
appropriate.example: Formal language was more appropriate than slang in the scholarship letter.
appropriate.basic: Formal language was a better fit than slang in the scholarship letter.

available.simple: Able to be used, seen, or obtained when needed.
available.detailed: Ready to be used, seen, or obtained when needed, rather than missing or already taken.
available.example: Only a small amount of clean water was available after the storm.
available.basic: Only a small amount of clean water could be used after the storm.

average.simple: Typical, or found by dividing a total by how many items there are.
average.detailed: Usual or ordinary, or the mean value calculated from a set of measurements.
average.example: The average temperature in June was two degrees lower than last year.
average.basic: The usual June temperature was two degrees lower than last year.

aware.simple: Knowing that something exists or is happening.
aware.detailed: Conscious of a fact, feeling, or risk, and able to take it into account.
aware.example: Oliver was aware that one weak paragraph could lower the whole mark.
aware.basic: Oliver knew that one weak paragraph could lower the whole mark.

brief.simple: Short in time or in the number of words.
brief.detailed: Lasting only a little while, or expressed in a compact way without extra detail.
brief.example: A brief summary of the method earned marks if every step was still clear.
brief.basic: A short summary of the method earned marks if every step was still clear.

capable.simple: Able to do a task well, with the needed skill.
capable.detailed: Having the skill, strength, or quality needed to achieve a task successfully.
capable.example: She proved capable of leading the group without talking over quieter voices.
capable.basic: She showed she could lead the group without talking over quieter voices.

central.simple: In the middle, or the most important idea or place.
central.detailed: Located at the centre, or forming the main idea around which other points are organised.
central.example: Fair sharing of water was the central idea in his persuasive speech.
central.basic: Fair sharing of water was the main idea in his persuasive speech.

certain.simple: Sure that something is true; or a particular one.
certain.detailed: Fully confident about a fact, or used to point to a specific but unnamed person or thing.
certain.example: The class was certain the leak came from the cracked join, not the tap.
certain.basic: The class was sure the leak came from the cracked join, not the tap.

considerable.simple: Fairly large or important in size or amount.
considerable.detailed: Great enough to notice and take seriously, though not necessarily the maximum possible.
considerable.example: The storm caused considerable damage to the coastal walking track.
considerable.basic: The storm caused quite a lot of damage to the coastal walking track.

consistent.simple: Always behaving or happening in the same way.
consistent.detailed: In agreement with previous results, rules, or claims, without unexplained contradictions.
consistent.example: The thermometer gave consistent readings when they repeated the trial.
consistent.basic: The thermometer gave the same readings when they repeated the trial.

constant.simple: Happening all the time, or not changing.
constant.detailed: Continuing without a break, or remaining the same while other variables change in an investigation.
constant.example: They kept the water volume constant so only the insulator could explain the result.
constant.basic: They kept the water volume the same so only the insulator could explain the result.

current.simple: Happening now, in the present time rather than the past.
current.detailed: Belonging to the present period rather than the past, as in today's events or today's policy.
current.example: The current water restrictions began after two dry summers.
current.basic: The water restrictions in force now began after two dry summers.

definite.simple: Clear and certain, leaving no room for vagueness.
definite.detailed: Fixed, exact, or unmistakable, leaving little room for doubt or other interpretations.
definite.example: She wanted a definite answer about whether the excursion would go ahead.
definite.basic: She wanted a clear yes or no about whether the excursion would go ahead.

detailed.simple: Including many facts, steps, and small points.
detailed.detailed: Thorough and specific, covering particulars rather than giving only a rough outline.
detailed.example: A detailed method let another group repeat the insulation test exactly.
detailed.basic: A full method let another group repeat the insulation test exactly.

distinct.simple: Clearly different, or easy to notice as separate.
distinct.detailed: Recognisably separate from something else, with features that set it apart.
distinct.example: The two frog calls were distinct enough for the class to tell them apart.
distinct.basic: The two frog calls were different enough for the class to tell them apart.

equal.simple: The same in amount, size, value, or rights.
equal.detailed: Having the same quantity or status, so one side is not greater or lesser than the other.
equal.example: Each farm was given an equal share of the extra water allocation.
equal.basic: Each farm was given the same share of the extra water.

exact.simple: Completely correct and accurate, with no error.
exact.detailed: Matching a true value or wording precisely, not roughly or approximately.
exact.example: The exact mass of the sample was 12.4 grams, not 'about twelve'.
exact.basic: The true mass of the sample was 12.4 grams, not 'about twelve'.

expected.simple: Thought likely to happen, based on what you already know.
expected.detailed: Predicted from evidence, a pattern, or a rule, and therefore not surprising if it occurs.
expected.example: The ice melted faster than expected when they used a black container.
expected.basic: The ice melted faster than they had thought when they used a black container.

extreme.simple: Very great in degree, far from ordinary or moderate.
extreme.detailed: Reaching a high degree or the outer limit, such as dangerous heat or a far-end opinion.
extreme.example: Extreme heat made the afternoon sports carnival unsafe.
extreme.basic: Very great heat made the afternoon sports carnival unsafe.

familiar.simple: Well known because you have seen or done it before.
familiar.detailed: Recognised from previous experience, and therefore easier to understand or use.
familiar.example: The creek path was familiar, but the flood had changed every bend.
familiar.basic: The creek path was well known, but the flood had changed every bend.

final.simple: Coming at the end of a sequence; the last one.
final.detailed: Occurring last in a sequence, or settling a matter so that no further change is planned.
final.example: His final draft cut the jokes that did not support the argument.
final.basic: His last draft cut the jokes that did not support the argument.

formal.simple: Following accepted rules of language or behaviour; not casual.
formal.detailed: Using the careful register expected in official writing, ceremonies, or academic tasks.
formal.example: A formal letter to the principal needed a greeting, a clear request, and a sign-off.
formal.basic: A careful letter to the principal needed a greeting, a clear request, and a sign-off.

frequent.simple: Happening often, many times in a short period.
frequent.detailed: Occurring many times in a period, rather than rarely or only once.
frequent.example: Frequent spelling errors in the same words pulled his mark down.
frequent.basic: Spelling errors that happened again and again pulled his mark down.

general.simple: True in most cases, not about one special example.
general.detailed: Broad or overall, applying to a whole group rather than to particular details.
general.example: The general rule was to save water, even if one garden looked dry.
general.basic: The broad rule was to save water, even if one garden looked dry.

gradual.simple: Happening slowly and steadily, a little at a time.
gradual.detailed: Changing by small steps rather than suddenly, so the shift is easy to miss at first.
gradual.example: The creek showed a gradual drop in water level across the dry month.
gradual.basic: The creek showed a slow drop in water level across the dry month.

immediate.simple: Happening at once, with no delay at all.
immediate.detailed: Occurring instantly, or next in time or space, with no gap in between.
immediate.example: The cracked pipe needed immediate action before more water was wasted.
immediate.basic: The cracked pipe needed action at once before more water was wasted.

independent.simple: Able to work or decide without relying on others.
independent.detailed: Not controlled by another person or country; able to act or think on one's own.
independent.example: After Federation the nation was still not fully independent of British law.
independent.basic: After Federation the nation still relied on some British law.

initial.simple: Happening at the beginning, before later changes.
initial.detailed: Coming first in time or in a sequence, before later changes or improvements.
initial.example: His initial plan was too vague, so he added two precise examples.
initial.basic: His first plan was too vague, so he added two precise examples.

likely.simple: Probably going to happen or turn out to be true.
likely.detailed: Having a good chance of occurring, based on evidence or a reasonable judgement.
likely.example: Rain is likely tomorrow if the clouds keep building from the south.
likely.basic: Rain will probably fall tomorrow if the clouds keep building from the south.

limited.simple: Not great in amount, number, time, or range.
limited.detailed: Restricted by a rule, resource, or ability, so there is a clear boundary on what is possible.
limited.example: They had limited time, so they tested only two insulators instead of five.
limited.basic: They did not have much time, so they tested only two insulators.

local.simple: Belonging to a nearby place or community.
local.detailed: Of a particular town, suburb, or region rather than the whole nation or world.
local.example: The local council voted to protect the remaining river red gums.
local.basic: The nearby council voted to protect the remaining river red gums.

logical.simple: Making sense because the reasons follow clearly.
logical.detailed: Organised according to sound reasoning, so each step follows from the one before.
logical.example: A logical conclusion names the evidence instead of jumping to a guess.
logical.basic: A sensible conclusion names the evidence instead of jumping to a guess.

major.simple: Very important or large compared with others.
major.detailed: Greater in size, rank, or significance than related things that are only minor.
major.example: Drought was a major reason families left the inland town.
major.basic: Drought was a main reason families left the inland town.

maximum.simple: The greatest possible amount, value, or number.
maximum.detailed: The highest value allowed or reached, often contrasted with a minimum.
maximum.example: The maximum temperature that week was 41 degrees in the inland town.
maximum.basic: The highest temperature that week was 41 degrees in the inland town.

minimum.simple: The smallest possible amount, value, or number.
minimum.detailed: The lowest value allowed or reached, often set as a required baseline.
minimum.example: The minimum night temperature dropped below zero on the tablelands.
minimum.basic: The lowest night temperature dropped below zero on the tablelands.

minor.simple: Smaller or less important than something else.
minor.detailed: Of lesser size, rank, or significance, and not the main factor in a result or story.
minor.example: A minor spelling error did not hide the strength of her argument.
minor.basic: A small spelling error did not hide the strength of her argument.

modern.simple: Belonging to the present time, not the distant past.
modern.detailed: Up to date in style, technology, or ideas, and contrasted with ancient or traditional ways.
modern.example: Modern Australia still debates how to recognise First Nations history.
modern.basic: Australia today still debates how to recognise First Nations history.

necessary.simple: Needed so badly that you cannot do without it.
necessary.detailed: Required for a result or duty to be completed, so leaving it out would cause failure or harm.
necessary.example: A labelled diagram was necessary to explain how the circuit worked.
necessary.basic: A labelled diagram was needed to explain how the circuit worked.

negative.simple: Harmful, unfavourable, or used to say no.
negative.detailed: Having a bad effect, expressing refusal, or falling below zero, depending on the subject.
negative.example: Plastic in the creek had a negative effect on the frogs' breeding sites.
negative.basic: Plastic in the creek harmed the frogs' breeding sites.

obvious.simple: Easy for almost anyone to see or understand.
obvious.detailed: So clear from the facts that little explanation is needed, though it may still need stating.
obvious.example: The most obvious reason the seedlings wilted was that the soil had dried out.
obvious.basic: The easiest reason to see for the wilted seedlings was that the soil had dried out.

official.simple: Approved by a person or group in authority.
official.detailed: Issued or recognised by a government, school, or other authorised body, not unofficial or rumoured.
official.example: The official rainfall figure came from the weather station, not from guesswork.
official.basic: The approved rainfall figure came from the weather station, not from guesswork.

ordinary.simple: Normal and everyday, not special or unusual.
ordinary.detailed: Typical of everyday life, without remarkable features, often used as a contrast in stories.
ordinary.example: The story began on an ordinary Saturday, which made the flood more shocking.
ordinary.basic: The story began on a normal Saturday, which made the flood more shocking.

original.simple: The first of its kind, or not copied from someone else.
original.detailed: Existing from the beginning, or newly invented rather than borrowed or imitated.
original.example: Her original opening was stronger than the copied quote she tried later.
original.basic: Her first opening was stronger than the copied quote she tried later.

overall.simple: Considering everything together, not just one part.
overall.detailed: Taking the whole situation into account, rather than focusing on one part only.
overall.example: The overall result favoured the wool insulator, even though one trial was messy.
overall.basic: When you looked at everything, wool still won, even though one trial was messy.

particular.simple: This one specifically, not a general case.
particular.detailed: Used to single out a definite person, thing, or feature from a larger group.
particular.example: That particular creek sample had far more salt than the others.
particular.basic: That one creek sample had far more salt than the others.

physical.simple: Of the body, or of things you can touch and measure.
physical.detailed: Relating to material objects and forces rather than ideas or feelings; also of bodily health.
physical.example: Melting ice is a physical change because the water can freeze again.
physical.basic: Melting ice is a change you can reverse by freezing the water again.

positive.simple: Helpful, hopeful, or used to agree and say yes.
positive.detailed: Having a good effect, expressing agreement, or greater than zero, depending on the subject.
positive.example: Planting trees along the bank had a positive effect on shade and bird life.
positive.basic: Planting trees along the bank helped shade and bird life.

possible.simple: Able to happen or be done if people try.
possible.detailed: Capable of occurring or being achieved, even if it is not certain or easy.
possible.example: A shorter shower is one possible way to cut household water use.
possible.basic: A shorter shower is one way you can cut household water use.

potential.simple: Possible in the future if conditions are right.
potential.detailed: Existing as a capacity or risk that has not yet been realised or proven.
potential.example: The old mine shaft was a potential danger, so the fence stayed locked.
potential.basic: The old mine shaft could become dangerous, so the fence stayed locked.

practical.simple: Useful in real life, not only in theory.
practical.detailed: Concerned with doing and applying ideas, or sensible given the tools and time you actually have.
practical.example: A bucket under the leak was a practical solution until the plumber arrived.
practical.basic: A bucket under the leak was a useful solution until the plumber arrived.

precise.simple: Exact and careful, with no vagueness left in.
precise.detailed: Accurate to a fine degree, using the right word, number, or measurement.
precise.example: A precise measurement of 12.4 grams is stronger than writing 'quite heavy'.
precise.basic: An exact measurement of 12.4 grams is stronger than writing 'quite heavy'.

previous.simple: Coming before this one in time or order.
previous.detailed: Existing or happening earlier, so it can be compared with the present case.
previous.example: The previous year's flood had already damaged the same walking bridge.
previous.basic: The year before, the flood had already damaged the same walking bridge.

primary.simple: First in order, or the most important of several.
primary.detailed: Main rather than secondary; also used for the earliest stage, such as a first-hand source.
primary.example: The primary reason the town grew was the new railway, not the shopfronts.
primary.basic: The main reason the town grew was the new railway, not the shopfronts.

private.simple: Belonging to one person or family, not to everyone.
private.detailed: Not open to the public, or kept personal rather than shared by the community or government.
private.example: The diary was a private record, so the class used only the published extracts.
private.basic: The diary was a personal record, so the class used only the published extracts.

probable.simple: More likely than not to be true or to happen.
probable.detailed: Supported by enough evidence to be a reasonable prediction, though not yet certain.
probable.example: A blocked drain was the probable cause of the flooded playground.
probable.basic: A blocked drain was the most likely cause of the flooded playground.

public.simple: Open to everyone, or belonging to the community.
public.detailed: Of the people as a whole, provided or seen by government or the community rather than kept private.
public.example: The new park is a public space, so dogs must stay on leads.
public.basic: The new park is open to everyone, so dogs must stay on leads.

rapid.simple: Happening very quickly, in a short space of time.
rapid.detailed: Taking place at high speed, often so fast that people or systems struggle to keep up.
rapid.example: The town saw rapid growth after the railway opened.
rapid.basic: The town grew very quickly after the railway opened.

rare.simple: Not happening or found very often in a place.
rare.detailed: Uncommon in number or frequency, and therefore noteworthy when it appears.
rare.example: The glossy black cockatoo is a rare visitor to that patch of woodland.
rare.basic: The glossy black cockatoo is an uncommon visitor to that woodland.

recent.simple: Having happened not long ago, close to now.
recent.detailed: Belonging to the near past, close enough to the present to still affect current events.
recent.example: Recent floods changed how the council plans the riverbank path.
recent.basic: Floods not long ago changed how the council plans the riverbank path.

regular.simple: Happening at even times, or following a usual pattern.
regular.detailed: Occurring at uniform intervals, or conforming to a rule, shape, or routine.
regular.example: They took temperature readings at regular ten-minute intervals.
regular.basic: They took temperature readings at even ten-minute intervals.

related.simple: Connected to something else by topic or cause.
related.detailed: Linked by cause, topic, family, or similarity, so the items should be considered together.
related.example: Salt in the soil is related to how much river water farmers pump.
related.basic: Salt in the soil is connected to how much river water farmers pump.

reliable.simple: Able to be trusted to work well or tell the truth.
reliable.detailed: Consistently accurate or dependable, so results or people can be used with confidence.
reliable.example: A labelled weather station is a more reliable source than a rumour at the shops.
reliable.basic: A labelled weather station is a more trustworthy source than a rumour at the shops.

responsible.simple: In charge of a duty, or careful about the effects of your actions.
responsible.detailed: Accountable for a task or outcome, and willing to act with care toward people or the environment.
responsible.example: Each group was responsible for packing up the science equipment.
responsible.basic: Each group was in charge of packing up the science equipment.

rural.simple: Of the countryside and farms, not the city.
rural.detailed: Relating to farming districts and small towns, with lower population density than urban areas.
rural.example: The rural school shared one bus route across three tiny towns.
rural.basic: The countryside school shared one bus route across three tiny towns.

scientific.simple: Using careful methods of investigation, or about science.
scientific.detailed: Based on observation, testing, and evidence rather than guesswork or opinion alone.
scientific.example: A scientific explanation names the evidence, not only what 'feels true'.
scientific.basic: A careful explanation names the evidence, not only what 'feels true'.

similar.simple: Almost the same as something else, but not identical.
similar.detailed: Sharing important features with something else while still remaining distinguishable.
similar.example: The two creeks showed a similar salt pattern after the dry season.
similar.basic: The two creeks showed almost the same salt pattern after the dry season.

social.simple: About people living and working together.
social.detailed: Relating to society, community life, or the way groups treat one another.
social.example: The gold rush caused rapid social change in the inland towns.
social.basic: The gold rush rapidly changed how people lived together in the inland towns.

stable.simple: Not likely to change, fall, or fail suddenly.
stable.detailed: Remaining steady over time, whether a structure, a population, or a set of measurements.
stable.example: The frog population stayed stable after the reeds were protected.
stable.basic: The frog numbers stayed steady after the reeds were protected.

strict.simple: Expecting rules to be followed exactly, with few exceptions.
strict.detailed: Enforcing standards firmly, with little room for exceptions or casual bending of the rules.
strict.example: The park had a strict limit of one bag of firewood per camp.
strict.basic: The park had a firm limit of one bag of firewood per camp.

successful.simple: Achieving what was wanted, planned, or aimed for.
successful.detailed: Producing the intended result, whether a test, a campaign, or a piece of writing.
successful.example: The recycling campaign was successful once every class had a clearly labelled bin.
successful.basic: The recycling campaign worked once every class had a clearly labelled bin.

suitable.simple: Right for a particular purpose or person.
suitable.detailed: Matching the needs of a situation, audience, or environment well enough to be a sound choice.
suitable.example: The reed bed was a suitable habitat for frogs after the bank was replanted.
suitable.basic: The reed bed was a good habitat for frogs after the bank was replanted.

typical.simple: Showing the usual features of a group or kind.
typical.detailed: Characteristic of a type, so it can stand as a fair example of the whole.
typical.example: A typical winter morning on the tablelands starts close to freezing.
typical.basic: A usual winter morning on the tablelands starts close to freezing.

unexpected.simple: Surprising because you did not think it would happen.
unexpected.detailed: Not predicted from the available evidence or pattern, and therefore needing explanation.
unexpected.example: The ice melted in an unexpected place: the shaded tray, not the sunny one.
unexpected.basic: The ice melted in a surprising place: the shaded tray, not the sunny one.

unusual.simple: Not common or not what you would normally expect.
unusual.detailed: Departing from the ordinary pattern, and therefore striking in a story or a data set.
unusual.example: An unusual silence in the bush made the hikers stop and listen.
unusual.basic: A strange silence in the bush made the hikers stop and listen.

valuable.simple: Worth a lot, either in money or in usefulness.
valuable.detailed: Having high worth because it is scarce, useful, or important to understanding or decision-making.
valuable.example: The old map was valuable evidence of where the first well had been dug.
valuable.basic: The old map was useful evidence of where the first well had been dug.

visible.simple: Able to be seen with the eyes, not hidden.
visible.detailed: Perceptible to the eye, or clear enough that people can notice it without special tools.
visible.example: The crack in the dam wall was visible from the lookout after the rain.
visible.basic: The crack in the dam wall could be seen from the lookout after the rain.

vital.simple: Absolutely necessary for success or for life.
vital.detailed: So important that the system, argument, or living thing cannot function well without it.
vital.zh: 至关重要的；必不可少的
vital.example: Clean water is vital to every living thing in the creek.
vital.basic: Clean water is essential to every living thing in the creek.

widespread.simple: Happening or found in many places, not just one.
widespread.detailed: Extending over a large area or among many people, not limited to one spot.
widespread.example: There was widespread support for a ban on single-use bottles at camp.
widespread.basic: Support for a ban on single-use bottles at camp came from many people.

renewable.simple: Able to be replaced naturally in a useful time.
renewable.detailed: Describes an energy source or resource that can replenish itself, unlike coal or oil.
renewable.example: Wind is a renewable energy source because the air keeps moving.
renewable.basic: Wind is an energy source that nature keeps replacing because the air keeps moving.

vivid.simple: Producing a strong, clear picture in the mind.
vivid.detailed: Bright, intense, or sharply described, so an image or memory feels almost present.
vivid.example: A vivid image of red dust on the washing line stayed with the reader.
vivid.basic: A strong picture of red dust on the washing line stayed with the reader.

abundant.simple: Present in a large amount, more than enough.
abundant.detailed: Plentiful enough that shortage is not the main problem, at least in that place or time.
abundant.example: After the wet spring there was abundant grass for the cattle.
abundant.basic: After the wet spring there was plenty of grass for the cattle.

credible.simple: Able to be believed because it seems honest and well supported.
credible.detailed: Convincing as a source or claim, based on evidence, expertise, or a fair method.
credible.example: A labelled graph is more credible than a claim with no numbers.
credible.basic: A labelled graph is easier to believe than a claim with no numbers.

cautious.simple: Careful to avoid danger, harm, or mistakes.
cautious.detailed: Acting with care because a risk is known, rather than rushing or guessing.
cautious.example: The hikers took a cautious step on the wet rocks above the falls.
cautious.basic: The hikers took a careful step on the wet rocks above the falls.

diligent.simple: Working hard and carefully over a long stretch of time.
diligent.detailed: Showing steady, attentive effort, especially on tasks that need accuracy.
diligent.example: A diligent check of every trial note caught the copied number.
diligent.basic: A hard, careful check of every trial note caught the copied number.

eager.simple: Wanting very much to do or have something.
eager.detailed: Keen and impatient in a hopeful way, showing strong interest or readiness.
eager.example: The class was eager to test the homemade compass on the oval.
eager.basic: The class really wanted to test the homemade compass on the oval.

enormous.simple: Extremely large in size, number, or amount.
enormous.detailed: So great that it stands far above ordinary scale, whether a creature, a number, or a problem.
enormous.example: There was an enormous difference between the sunny tray and the shaded one.
enormous.basic: There was a huge difference between the sunny tray and the shaded one.

generous.simple: Happy to give more than is strictly needed.
generous.detailed: Willing to share time, money, or kindness freely, beyond the minimum duty.
generous.example: A generous neighbour filled the tanks when the bore failed.
generous.basic: A kind neighbour filled the tanks when the bore failed.

honest.simple: Telling the truth and refusing to cheat or hide facts.
honest.detailed: Sincere and fair in words and actions, even when the truth is uncomfortable.
honest.example: An honest account of the broken beaker earned more trust than a hidden excuse.
honest.basic: A truthful account of the broken beaker earned more trust than a hidden excuse.

magnificent.simple: Extremely impressive and beautiful in a grand way.
magnificent.detailed: Grand in appearance or quality, inspiring admiration for scale, colour, or skill.
magnificent.example: From the ridge they saw a magnificent view of the flooded river flats.
magnificent.basic: From the ridge they saw a stunning view of the flooded river flats.

patient.simple: Able to wait or keep trying without getting angry.
patient.detailed: Calmly enduring delay, difficulty, or another person's pace, without complaint.
patient.example: A patient listener let the younger speaker finish before asking questions.
patient.basic: A calm listener let the younger speaker finish before asking questions.

peculiar.simple: Strange or unusual, not like what you expect.
peculiar.detailed: Odd in a noticeable way, or belonging specially to one person, place, or thing.
peculiar.example: A peculiar smell near the drain made the class stop the water test.
peculiar.basic: A strange smell near the drain made the class stop the water test.

thorough.simple: Complete and careful, leaving nothing important out.
thorough.detailed: Done with close attention to every relevant part, so gaps and errors are less likely.
thorough.example: A thorough check of the method showed they had forgotten to dry the thermometer.
thorough.basic: A complete check of the method showed they had forgotten to dry the thermometer.

urban.simple: Of a city or large town, not the countryside.
urban.detailed: Relating to built-up areas with dense housing, transport, and services, contrasted with rural life.
urban.example: Urban growth pushed new houses onto the last market gardens.
urban.basic: City growth pushed new houses onto the last market gardens.

coastal.simple: On or near the sea, along a stretch of coast.
coastal.detailed: Located along a coastline, shaped by tides, wind, and the meeting of land and ocean.
coastal.example: Coastal erosion ate away the walking path after the spring tides.
coastal.basic: The sea ate away the walking path after the spring tides.

global.simple: Relating to the whole world, not just one country.
global.detailed: Involving every region of Earth, or considering an issue at world scale rather than locally.
global.example: Plastic waste is a global issue, even when it starts in one creek.
global.basic: Plastic waste is a worldwide issue, even when it starts in one creek.

national.simple: Of a whole country, not just one town or district.
national.detailed: Relating to a country as a single political or cultural unit, such as a country-wide park or parliament.
national.example: Uluru–Kata Tjuta is a national park jointly managed with Traditional Owners.
national.basic: Uluru–Kata Tjuta is a park for the whole country, jointly managed with Traditional Owners.

cultural.simple: About the customs, arts, and beliefs of a group of people.
cultural.detailed: Relating to shared ways of life—language, ceremony, stories, and art—that give a community identity.
cultural.example: Dance can be a cultural tradition that teaches history as well as steps.
cultural.basic: Dance can be a community custom that teaches history as well as steps.

historical.simple: About the past, or based on real events in the past.
historical.detailed: Connected with history as a record of what happened, as opposed to purely imaginary stories.
historical.example: A letter from 1901 is historical evidence of how Federation felt to ordinary voters.
historical.basic: A letter from 1901 is evidence from the past of how Federation felt to ordinary voters.

political.simple: About government, power, and how decisions are made for a community.
political.detailed: Relating to parties, laws, elections, and the struggle over who holds authority.
political.example: Federation was a political change as well as a change of maps.
political.basic: Federation changed who held power, not only where the borders were drawn.

economic.simple: About money, jobs, trade, and how a community uses resources.
economic.detailed: Relating to the production, distribution, and use of goods and services, including costs and livelihoods.
economic.example: The drought had an economic impact on shops as well as on farms.
economic.basic: The drought hurt shops as well as farms because people had less money.

legal.simple: Allowed by law, or concerned with the law itself.
legal.detailed: Required, permitted, or decided under a system of laws, as opposed to illegal or merely moral.
legal.example: Children have a legal right to a safe school, not only a hoped-for one.
legal.basic: Children have a right in law to a safe school, not only a hoped-for one.

moral.simple: About what is right or wrong in how people treat others.
moral.detailed: Concerned with principles of fairness, honesty, and duty, rather than only with what is legal.
moral.example: Leaving rubbish in the creek was a moral failure, not only a messy habit.
moral.basic: Leaving rubbish in the creek was wrong, not only a messy habit.

ethical.simple: Following fair rules about how people ought to act.
ethical.detailed: Guided by principles of honesty and respect, especially when a choice could help or harm others.
ethical.example: Copying a classmate's results is not an ethical way to finish a report.
ethical.basic: Copying a classmate's results is not a fair way to finish a report.

financial.simple: About money and how it is earned, spent, or saved.
financial.detailed: Relating to funds, costs, banks, or household and government budgets.
financial.example: The financial cost of a new well was too high for one family alone.
financial.basic: The money cost of a new well was too high for one family alone.

technical.simple: About specialised methods, tools, or skills.
technical.detailed: Involving the detailed working of a system, machine, or field, often with precise vocabulary.
technical.example: Density is a technical term for how much mass fits into a given volume.
technical.basic: Density is a specialist word for how much mass fits into a given volume.

visual.simple: Related to seeing with the eyes, or to images.
visual.detailed: Perceived by the eyes, or created as a picture, diagram, or other image that carries meaning.
visual.example: The poster used a strong visual image of a dry dam to argue for shorter showers.
visual.basic: The poster used a strong picture of a dry dam to argue for shorter showers.

mental.simple: Of the mind and thinking, not of the body.
mental.detailed: Relating to thinking, memory, or psychological health, as opposed to physical action.
mental.example: A clear mental picture of the water cycle helped her explain each stage.
mental.basic: A clear picture in her mind of the water cycle helped her explain each stage.

emotional.simple: About strong feelings, or showing them clearly.
emotional.detailed: Connected with emotions such as fear, joy, or grief, and how those feelings shape behaviour or writing.
emotional.example: The farewell scene was so emotional that several readers went quiet.
emotional.basic: The farewell scene was so full of feeling that several readers went quiet.

personal.simple: About one particular person, or belonging to them.
personal.detailed: Private or individual rather than public or general, often based on a person's own experience.
personal.example: A personal story about the flood made the speech more convincing than statistics alone.
personal.basic: A story from her own life about the flood made the speech more convincing than statistics alone.

professional.simple: Doing a job with trained skill, or suitable for that kind of work.
professional.detailed: Relating to a paid occupation that requires training, or showing the careful standards of such work.
professional.example: They asked for professional advice before testing the old well water.
professional.basic: They asked for trained expert advice before testing the old well water.

traditional.simple: Following customs that have been kept for a long time.
traditional.detailed: Based on practices handed down through generations, rather than on the newest fashion or method.
traditional.example: The class read a traditional story about how the river was formed.
traditional.basic: The class read a long-kept story about how the river was formed.

digital.simple: Using computers or electronic technology; made of digits.
digital.detailed: Stored or transmitted as electronic data, as opposed to paper, analogue film, or face-to-face only.
digital.example: A digital photograph of the creek can be compared with the same bend next year.
digital.basic: An electronic photograph of the creek can be compared with the same bend next year.

long-term.simple: Lasting or planned for a long time into the future.
long-term.detailed: Extending over many months or years, rather than solving only the problem in front of you now.
long-term.example: Planting trees is a long-term plan for cooler streets, not a one-week fix.
long-term.basic: Planting trees is a plan for cooler streets over many years, not a one-week fix.

short-term.simple: Lasting or planned for only a short time.
short-term.detailed: Useful in the near future, but not necessarily solving the deeper or lasting problem.
short-term.example: A water truck is a short-term fix until the broken pipe is replaced.
short-term.basic: A water truck helps for now until the broken pipe is replaced.

first-hand.simple: Experienced or seen by the person themselves.
first-hand.detailed: Gained by direct observation or participation, not reported by someone else.
first-hand.example: A first-hand account of the flood from a farmer is stronger than a rumour.
first-hand.basic: An account from a farmer who saw the flood is stronger than a rumour.

well-known.simple: Known by many people, not hidden or obscure.
well-known.detailed: Familiar to a wide audience because of fame, frequent use, or public discussion.
well-known.example: The well-known story of the stolen generations still shocks new readers.
well-known.basic: The famous story of the stolen generations still shocks new readers.

evidence-based.simple: Built on tested facts rather than guesses.
evidence-based.detailed: Supported by collected data, observation, or research, so a claim can be checked.
evidence-based.example: An evidence-based claim about recycling names the school's actual bin data.
evidence-based.basic: A claim about recycling that uses facts names the school's actual bin data.

age-old.simple: Having existed for a very long time, not recently invented.
age-old.detailed: So long established that it feels part of a culture or landscape, not a recent invention.
age-old.example: Sharing water in a dry country is an age-old problem, not only a modern one.
age-old.basic: Sharing water in a dry country is a very old problem, not only a modern one.

clearly.simple: In a way that is easy to see, hear, or understand.
clearly.detailed: With no confusion, so a reader or listener can follow the idea without guessing.
clearly.example: The diagram clearly showed which way the current travelled in the circuit.
clearly.basic: The diagram showed in an easy way which way the current travelled.

directly.simple: In a straight way, without going around or delaying.
directly.detailed: With no intervening step, person, or detour; immediately or in a frank manner.
directly.example: The question was directly related to the data in the table, not to a side story.
directly.basic: The question was straight about the data in the table, not about a side story.

effectively.simple: In a way that works well and gets the intended result.
effectively.detailed: Producing the desired outcome with suitable methods, not merely looking busy.
effectively.example: Shorter showers effectively reduced the camp's water use in one week.
effectively.basic: Shorter showers reduced the camp's water use in one week.

eventually.simple: After a period of time has passed; in the end.
eventually.detailed: At a later point, after delay, effort, or a sequence of events, the outcome occurs.
eventually.example: The missing compass eventually turned up in the bottom of the sports bag.
eventually.basic: The missing compass turned up in the end in the bottom of the sports bag.

generally.simple: In most cases, or considering the whole rather than exceptions.
generally.detailed: Usually or on the whole, allowing that a few cases may differ from the main pattern.
generally.example: Frogs are generally more active after rain, though a few species differ.
generally.basic: Frogs are usually more active after rain, though a few kinds differ.

gradually.simple: Slowly and steadily, changing a little at a time.
gradually.detailed: By small degrees rather than all at once, so the change accumulates over time.
gradually.example: The puddle gradually disappeared as the sun warmed the oval.
gradually.basic: The puddle disappeared little by little as the sun warmed the oval.

immediately.simple: At once, without any wait or pause at all.
immediately.detailed: Happening in the next instant, with no delay between cause and action or result.
immediately.example: They stopped the trial immediately after the beaker cracked.
immediately.basic: They stopped the trial at once after the beaker cracked.

mainly.simple: For the most part; more than anything else.
mainly.detailed: Chiefly or primarily, indicating the largest share or the most important reason.
mainly.example: The town grew mainly because the railway opened, not because of one shop.
mainly.basic: The town grew mostly because the railway opened, not because of one shop.
